inbox.content: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.

history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx), proposed by Harvard University, aimed to investigate the behavior of small aerosol particles in the stratosphere. Led by principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators such as David Keith, SCoPEx was publicly discussed at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. The initiative was focused on enhancing computer models to assess the potential risks and benefits associated with solar geoengineering, specifically solar radiation management, but it was not intended as a deployment of geoengineering or as a means to cool the planet. The experiment involved a scientific balloon gondola operating at approximately 20 km altitude, releasing a minimal amount of material—around 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms—typically calcium carbonate, into a defined volume. A 2021 test in Sweden was limited to hardware assessment, with the SCoPEx Advisory Committee advising a pause until societal engagement could be achieved. In March 2024, Harvard announced that Keutsch would no longer pursue SCoPEx, indicating a shift towards repurposing the platform for different stratospheric research unrelated to solar geoengineering.

history.contentIn: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) is a proposed solar radiation modification method that would introduce aerosols into the stratosphere to reflect a small fraction of incoming sunlight, analogous in mechanism to cooling after large volcanic eruptions such as Mount Pinatubo in 1991. Candidate materials discussed in the literature include sulfates and, in some proposals, calcite or other particles. Delivery concepts include specialised high-altitude aircraft; there is no operational global SAI deployment. SAI would not remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, would not stop ocean acidification, and would require a sustained commitment if used to offset continued high emissions. Risks discussed in assessments include ozone chemistry, changes in precipitation patterns, termination shock if a program stopped abruptly, and governance problems. Small research proposals such as Harvard's SCoPEx aimed to measure aerosol microphysics in a tiny plume, not to cool the planet. Public claims that routine commercial aviation is already injecting SAI materials as 'chemtrails' are not supported by atmospheric science.

Meeting Paris temperature goals requires deep, sustained cuts in fossil CO2, methane and other greenhouse gases, plus protection of carbon sinks — not covert aviation spraying.

history.contentIn: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.
